1. The verb in first position instead of “wenn”
You can leave out “wenn” and put the conjugated verb in first position. The second clause often begins with “dann” or “so”, or directly with the verb.
Wenn es regnet, feiern wir drinnen.
Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, wäre ich gekommen.
Hätte ich das gewusst, wäre ich gekommen.
Wenn er zu spät kommt, fangen wir ohne ihn an.
Kommt er zu spät, fangen wir ohne ihn an.
Don't confuse this with a question: “Regnet es?” (question) vs. “Regnet es, feiern wir drinnen.” (condition). The second clause makes the difference.
Should you have any questions, please call us.
“Sollten Sie Fragen haben” is the classic phrase at the end of formal emails. You'll see it everywhere.
Falls Grete müde ist, gehen wir früher.
Sofern das Wetter hält, feiern wir draußen.
Im Falle, dass der Strom ausfällt, …
Wir feiern draußen, es sei denn, es gewittert.
“Es sei denn” is followed by a main clause (verb in second position), separated by a comma: “…, es sei denn, es gewittert.”
In the event of a storm, the party will take place in the café.
In case of rain, the picnic is cancelled.

It was raining. Of course it was raining. At six in the morning, on Saturday, the seventh of June two thousand and thirty-six, when Lena woke up, because she hadn't slept since four, the rain was beating on the windowsill on the first floor of number thirty-one, so hard and so steadily, as if it intended to stay all day. Lena lay in bed and listened. Next to her Andrei was sleeping, peacefully, on his back, with a faint smile, like a man who had never read a weather forecast in his whole life. Lena looked at her phone. Sixty per cent, the app had said yesterday. Today it said: ninety. Had she known that June in Berlin could be so wet, Lena thought, she would have chosen May. But May had been Grete's birthday. And Grete had said: “Take an early Saturday in June.” So they had taken this one.

At half past six, Lena was standing in the kitchen and declared, as she had agreed with everyone beforehand, “plan B”. She called it out into the stairwell, not very loudly, but loudly enough for a door to open on the ground floor and for Ludwig to appear in his dressing gown, with a cup of coffee and an expression as if he had been waiting for this moment for hours. “Plan B,” he repeated, pleased. “Very good. I've never yet been to a wedding where plan A worked. Including my own.” Then he went back into his flat to get dressed, and Lena heard him laughing softly on the stairs. She didn't know that Ludwig, Hotte and Andrei had already made a plan of their own a week ago, in case it rained. A plan C. And that this plan C had nothing to do with the café.

At first plan B went as planned. At seven Michael Kühn and Leo came and carried the three long tables, which were already standing in the courtyard under the chestnut tree, into the café, which was closed that day, with a sign on the door: “Heute wegen Hochzeit geschlossen. Klingeln trotzdem erlaubt.” (Closed today for a wedding. Ringing the bell allowed anyway.) At eight Ayşe Yilmaz and Sabine came with the flowers, white peonies from Frau Lorenz's garden in Thuringia, which she had brought in person the evening before. At nine Mara came and announced that Grete had had a good night, that she had eaten breakfast, “even half a bread roll”, and that she insisted on wearing her black hat, although Frau Petersen had offered her a rain hat. “If it rains on my hat,” Grete had apparently said, “then it rains on my hat. I'm a hundred years old. I'm not letting the weather tell me what to wear any more.”

The ceremony was at eleven at the Pankow registry office. At a quarter past ten, Lena stood in front of the bedroom mirror, in a simple cream-coloured dress that Elena had sewn in Sibiu, with a narrow strip of embroidery at the collar, following the pattern of the same blouse from which she had also embroidered Mara's wedding dress. On her right hand Lena wore the little silver ring with the bee that Andrei had given her seven years ago, when they weren't yet together, and on her left the gold one from Sibiu. Sabine stood behind her and pinned a white peony in her hair, with trembling fingers. “If your grandmother were here,” Sabine said softly, “she'd say something wise now. Some quotation from a book.” Lena looked at her mother in the mirror. “She'd say: whoever reads is never completely alone,” she said. “And neither is whoever gets married.”

At half past ten, when Lena came down the stairs, she heard something she wasn't expecting. A bell. Not the brass bell from the café but another one, louder, deeper, ringing out along the whole of Kastanienallee, twice, three times, like a signal. She opened the front door. And in front of the door, in the street, in the rain, on the tracks of the M1 line, stood a tram. An old tram, red and beige, with round headlights and the number 5218 on its side, and on the destination board above the windscreen, in white letters, it said not “Hackescher Markt” and not “Pankow” but: “Standesamt. Sonderfahrt.” (Registry office. Special service.) In the cab sat Kurt Wolff, in his old uniform, and next to him, with his tram driver's cap on his head and a grin from ear to ear, Hotte.

That was plan C. Kurt Wolff had taken the Tatra 5218 out of the tram museum, the same tram in which Ludwig had driven the number 46 route once more in October two thousand and twenty-seven. The permit for the special service had taken three weeks and, as Kurt Wolff admitted later, “two forms in very good bureaucratic German”. The idea had been Hotte's. “If it rains,” he had said a week ago, “then the bride ain't goin' by taxi. Then she's goin' by tram. Like her gran in nineteen sixty-nine. Only this time no books fall out.” Ludwig had first said no, then maybe, then yes. Andrei had kept quiet the whole week, which, as he put it, had been harder than his master's degree.

Lena stood in the doorway and couldn't say anything. The rain was falling on the red tram, on the round headlights, on the board with the word “Standesamt”. Behind her Ludwig came down the stairs, in his good grey suit, with a white peony in his buttonhole, and put his hand on her shoulder. “Plan C,” he said. “If I'd told you, you'd have made a plan D.” Then he offered her his arm and they went out together, under a big black umbrella that Leo held over them, across the wet pavement, towards the open door of the tram. Hotte rang once more, twice, and called from the cab: “All aboard, please! Nobody gets left on the platform today!”

Everyone was already sitting in the tram. Andrei was sitting right at the front, in a dark blue suit, with a white peony in his buttonhole and an expression as if he had just passed a very hard exam. Next to him, Dan and Elena, who had come from Sibiu on Thursday, Dan in a tie he hadn't worn since his own wedding and which, as Elena remarked in a whisper, “still smells of beeswax”. Thomas and Anja, Paul, Marie. Mara and Jakob with Ingrid Hilde on their lap, who was looking out of the window at the rain with big eyes and holding the little velvet box with the two rings tightly in both hands. Elif with her mother. Dr Vogt, who had swapped his night shift. Katrin Krüger, without her notebook, with tissues. And in the second row, in her wheelchair strapped to the floor, Grete, with her black hat with the feather, on which not a single raindrop had fallen.

The ride took eleven minutes. Kurt Wolff drove slowly, much more slowly than the timetable would have allowed, but that day there was no timetable. The tram went up Kastanienallee, through the rain, past Ingrid-Brandt-Platz, where Frau Becker from the kiosk stood with an umbrella and waved, along Schönhauser Allee, past the Milastraße stop, where Leo had braked in March and where now a little boy in a red jacket was holding his mother's hand and staring open-mouthed after the old tram. People on the pavements stopped. Cars honked. A cyclist rang back. And in the tram someone was singing, softly at first, then louder, and then everyone sang, German and Romanian mixed together, and Grete tapped out the beat with her finger on the armrest of her wheelchair.

In the wedding room Frau Kranz was waiting, in a dark green suit, with a folder in which, along with all the documents, there was a small yellow sticky note. She gave a short speech, without a single word of bureaucratic German, about two people from two countries who had found each other in a house in Berlin, “because an old lady with bees and an old gentleman with trams were of the opinion that doors exist to be opened”. Then she asked the question. She asked Andrei first. “Herr Andrei Ionescu, do you wish to take Lena Brandt, here present, as your wife? Then answer yes.” Andrei answered. He answered with “Ja”. And then, after a little pause, so quietly that only the first rows heard it, once more: “Da.” (Romanian for “yes”.) Frau Kranz smiled. “Both are valid,” she said.

Then came the moment with the rings, and with it the only part of the day for which there was no plan, neither A nor B nor C. Mara put Ingrid Hilde down, and Ingrid Hilde, sixteen months old, who had been able to walk for two weeks, even if not very far, stood for a moment, unsure, with the little velvet box in both hands. The whole room held its breath. Then she set off. Not towards Andrei. Not towards Lena. But diagonally across the room, with small, wobbly steps, towards the second row, towards Grete, and put the little box in her lap. Grete looked at the child, then at the box, then into the room, and her face showed something between laughing and crying. Then she took the box, with both trembling hands, and held it out to Lena. “A hundred years,” she said, loudly enough for everyone to hear, “and for the first time I'm a ring bearer.”

When they came out of the registry office as husband and wife, Lena Brandt-Ionescu and Andrei Ionescu, the rain had stopped. Not completely. It was still drizzling, a fine, warm June rain, and between the clouds above Pankow the sun was breaking through in one spot, and on the other side of the sky, above the rooftops towards Prenzlauer Berg, there was a rainbow, pale but complete, from one end to the other. The old tram was waiting outside the door. Kurt Wolff rang. Hotte rang. And then, from the second row, through the open window, someone else rang: Grete, who had asked Mara to let her reach the cord of the emergency bell and who now, with her trembling hundred-year-old hand, pulled the cord twice. Once for the bride and groom. And once, as she explained later, for Friedrich, who had surely been listening today.

In the evening they celebrated in the courtyard after all. The sun came out completely at about five, the cobbles dried in half an hour, and Leo and Michael carried the three long tables back outside, under the chestnut tree, which had already finished flowering but was full of green leaves in which raindrops still hung, sparkling in the light. Lena watched the tables going back to their place and laughed. “Plan A,” she said to Andrei. “In the end it was plan A that worked after all. Just seven hours later.” Andrei took her hand, the one with the two rings. “If we'd only had plan A,” he said, “we wouldn't have had a tram. Or a rainbow. And Grete would never have been a ring bearer.” Lena thought about it. Then she said: “If we ever plan anything again, we'll start with plan C.”
